data.title: Anthropic IPO haul hits $93.5B: buy ANT on the pullback?
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) added $12.2 billion to its record IPO haul this morning while investors “marked down” the shares.

Underwriters exercised their option to buy additional ANT stock, lifting the company’s gross IPO proceeds to a whopping $93.5 billion.

Meanwhile, Anthropic shares tanked over 9% in trading on Friday, after closing its Nasdaq debut at $97.17.

The extra cash gives the Claude maker more room to fund its expansion.

For buyers weighing the dip, the question is how much of that spending can eventually turn into cash flow.

What Anthropic actually gets from the $93.5 billion IPO

The extra $12.2 billion is especially valuable because all 147 million shares sold through the underwriters’ option were newly issued by Anthropic at $83 apiece.

Existing shareholders sold a portion of the original offering, so some of that money went to them.

The prospectus puts Anthropic’s own net proceeds at about $117 billion after offering costs, including a separate $26 billion private placement.

The trade-off for shareholders is straightforward.

The additional issuance increases the post-deal share count by about 1.1% compared with the base offering, so each share represents a slightly smaller ownership stake.

In exchange, Anthropic has more cash to secure computing capacity and hire researchers without having to return to the market as quickly if AI stocks stay under pressure.

The bigger number on Anthropic’s books is its compute bill

Anthropic disclosed roughly $900 billion in computing commitments, with about $70.7 billion due in the 12 months after Sept. 30. That gives the extra IPO cash some scale.

The $12.2 billion covers the equivalent of about two months of those near-term commitments, assuming payments were spread evenly.

The commitments extend over many years, but the near-term figure shows how quickly a record capital raise can be put to work.

Demand for Claude is already substantial. Third-quarter revenue reached $17 billion, more than 12 times the year-earlier figure.

Anthropic still posted a $567 million operating loss, driven in part by short-term compute costs.

Investors should watch whether operating margins improve as more businesses use Claude, especially once the capacity Anthropic has already committed to starts coming online.

Is ANT stock worth buying on Friday’s pullback?

Friday’s retreat makes ANT more attractive than it was at Thursday’s $111.50 opening trade.

At the premarket level, the shares are still roughly 5% above the $83 offer price.

That gap shows how much of the debut premium has evaporated in less than two sessions.

The IPO price itself offers little guidance on what investors should pay for the business over the long run.

The case for waiting is stronger. Anthropic has secured more of the money it needs to expand, and Claude’s revenue growth shows customers are willing to pay.

The next test is whether Anthropic can keep more of each dollar it brings in as its computing bills rise.

Evidence of that in its first earnings report as a public company would make a stronger case for buying ANT than Friday’s discount alone.

data.title: Coinbase opens Deribit-powered crypto options to non-US retail traders
data.description:
Coinbase has opened crypto options trading to eligible retail customers outside the US, routing orders through Deribit, the derivatives exchange it acquired in 2025.

The exchange said on X on 19 November 2026 that options were "available now on Coinbase" and "powered by Deribit's deep global liquidity".

Chief executive Brian Armstrong said the product was live for non-US users and was "coming to the US soon with Coinbase Pro". He did not give a date.

The move brings Deribit's order book to Coinbase's own retail interface. Earlier this month, Invezz reported that Coinbase Prime had opened Deribit options and perpetuals to eligible US institutions.

Six assets, settled in USDC

According to Coinbase's help centre, customers can trade options on Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), Avalanche (AVAX), Hyperliquid (HYPE) and XRP.

The contracts are linear options, executed on Deribit infrastructure and settled in the USDC stablecoin. Each is named by underlying asset, expiry date, strike price and type.

Trading takes place in Coinbase Advanced, the exchange's order-book interface. A market information panel shows contract size, minimum order size, tick size and settlement currency.

Multi-leg orders in one step

Coinbase is also offering "combo" order books, which let traders execute every leg of a strategy, such as a call spread, straddle or iron condor, in a single order at one price.

The company says all legs fill together, so one leg cannot execute while the price moves away from the other. Minimum combo sizes match the underlying options, for example 0.01 BTC or 0.1 ETH.

Combos are available for selected USDC-settled options, and availability depends on asset, expiry, strikes and region, Coinbase said. In October, it said the order screen would include a payoff diagram showing breakeven points.

Who can trade

Access is restricted. Coinbase says its Global Derivatives offering is available only to eligible customers in select regions outside the US, and requires an existing Coinbase spot account.

Customers answer onboarding and verification questions in the app, then fund a derivatives portfolio with USDC, BTC, ETH or other accepted collateral. Coinbase has not published a full list of supported countries.

In Australia, the product is open only to wholesale investors. They must supply an accountant's certificate showing net assets of at least A$2.5 million or gross income of at least A$250,000 a year.

For most eligible customers, the broker is Coinbase Bermuda, which is regulated by the Bermuda Monetary Authority and is a member of the Deribit exchange. Deribit is operated by Deribit FZE under a licence from Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority.

The Deribit bet

Coinbase completed its purchase of Deribit on 14 August 2025, in a deal valued at about $2.9B when it was announced. At the time, Coinbase called Deribit the largest crypto options exchange by volume and open interest.

On 7 October 2026, Coinbase said the Deribit integration was complete. It said customers would gain access to liquidity holding more than $30B in Bitcoin options open interest, as of 30 September.

That announcement said options would reach eligible traders outside the US "in the coming weeks", with US retail access "later this year". Coinbase said in a follow-up post on 19 November that Deribit does not offer its services in the US.

What it means for traders

For non-US customers already on Coinbase, the launch removes the need to open a separate account with a specialist options venue to trade listed crypto options.

The product is narrower than Deribit's full market, however. CryptoSlate, citing Deribit's monthly statistics, reported that USDC-settled options made up about 2% of Deribit's October options turnover, with coin-settled BTC and ETH contracts accounting for the rest.

The launch also puts Coinbase in more direct competition with other large crypto exchanges, including Binance, that already offer options to retail customers in some markets.

Options can expire worthless, and sellers can face losses well beyond the premium received. Coinbase's own documentation warns that some combo strategies carry unlimited risk.

data.title: Intuit stock falls 9% on FY27 revenue forecast cut, Mailchimp sale; analysts cut PTs
data.description:
Intuit shares (NASDAQ: INTU) fell more than 9% in premarket trading on Friday after the financial technology company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast and announced the sale of its email marketing platform Mailchimp to Italian technology group Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion.

The sell-off came despite a stronger-than-expected first-quarter earnings performance, as investors focused on weaker revenue expectations and slowing growth at Credit Karma.

The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91 for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended October 31, representing a 56% increase from $1.87 a year earlier.

The figure exceeded S&P Global Market Intelligence's CapIQ estimate of $2.64.

Revenue rose 12% year-over-year to $4.4 billion, also beating Visible Alpha's consensus estimate of $4.31 billion.

However, the stronger quarterly performance failed to offset concerns about the company's outlook.

Intuit now expects full-year revenue growth of 8%-9%, compared with its previous forecast of 9%-10%.

The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to a range of $23.08 billion to $23.37 billion, from its earlier projection of $23.28 billion to $23.51 billion.

The revised range also falls short of Visible Alpha's consensus estimate of $23.40 billion.

Credit Karma slowdown prompts Intuit to cut revenue outlook

The downgrade was primarily driven by weaker-than-expected performance at Credit Karma, Intuit's personal finance platform.

The company attributed the slowdown to a combination of higher interest rates, softer consumer demand, and changing user behaviour, particularly as consumers increasingly engage with artificial intelligence-powered experiences.

Speaking to Seeking Alpha, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla said the macroeconomic environment had changed since the company established its guidance in August.

"One is the interest rate environment is different today than when we set guidance in August. In August, we were debating whether the Fed will hold interest rates or drop interest rates."

"After the September interest rate increase, we saw consumer demand across our verticals slow down," said the CFO.

"Late in the quarter, we saw our partner's pace of growth in the segments we serve slow down."

Aujla also pointed to the faster-than-anticipated impact of changing consumer behaviour as more users turn to AI-powered experiences.

"And then, we saw the evolution in consumer behavior, particularly in how they're engaging with AI experiences, having a larger than anticipated or faster than anticipated impact on our performance. So these are factors that are impacting us here in the near term."

He added that Credit Karma was one of the company's businesses most exposed to macroeconomic cycles.

"Credit Karma is one part of our company that is impacted by the macro cycle," the CFO said.

Intuit maintained its full-year operating income and profit guidance, suggesting that the revised revenue outlook has not yet translated into a broader reduction in its profitability expectations.

Nevertheless, the Credit Karma weakness has raised concerns about the company's ability to maintain growth across its different business segments.

Intuit sells Mailchimp for $3.68 billion after $12 billion acquisition

In a separate development, Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion, five years after acquiring the email marketing platform for around $12 billion.

The transaction includes $3.31 billion in cash and $368 million in stock and is expected to close in early 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

The sale represents a substantial reduction from the price Intuit paid in 2021, when it completed its largest acquisition to expand its portfolio of small-business software and marketing services.

Intuit said the divestiture would allow it to sharpen its focus on AI-powered products for small businesses. The company also plans to use the cash proceeds to repurchase shares.

"Mailchimp has helped millions of businesses grow and acquire customers through email marketing automation," said Jack Tam, senior vice president at Intuit.

However, the platform has struggled to deliver growth recently.

Mailchimp's revenue declined 1% year-over-year to $313 million in the first quarter.

The acquisition also highlights the challenges Intuit has faced in extracting value from its large investments in business software.

For Bending Spoons, the transaction adds another major digital platform to its expanding portfolio.

The company, which went public in July, said it intends to invest substantially in Mailchimp and pursue changes across its technology, products, marketing and monetisation strategies.

The divestiture is part of Intuit's broader strategy to integrate artificial intelligence into its products and automate tasks for consumers and businesses.

The company has increasingly prioritised AI-powered services as it seeks to expand its offerings and improve productivity for customers.

Wall Street analysts cut Intuit price targets after results

The combination of weaker revenue guidance, Credit Karma's slowdown and uncertainty surrounding AI disruption prompted several Wall Street firms to lower their price targets on Intuit.

The stock is down 50% so far this year.

Morgan Stanley reduced its price target to $310 from $315 while maintaining an Equalweight rating.

The brokerage acknowledged strong execution in Intuit's Global Business Solutions segment and better-than-expected earnings.

However, it said these positives were overshadowed by the Credit Karma-led revenue downgrade and weaker second-quarter guidance.

"Strong GBS and EPS execution were overshadowed by a Credit Karma-led FY27 revenue cut and weak Q2 guide," Morgan Stanley said in a note.

The firm viewed the Mailchimp divestiture as strategically positive but flagged risks associated with AI-driven customer discovery and execution in Intuit's tax business.

Barclays also lowered its price target, cutting it to $385 from $408 while maintaining an Overweight rating.

The brokerage described Credit Karma as "now also a major segment that needs fixing," according to a note cited by TheFly.

Barclays expects near-term pressure on the shares, saying it was "not sure there is a short-term comeback here", although it also described the stock as "cheap."

Jefferies lowered its target to $445 from $500 while retaining a Buy recommendation.

The brokerage described the quarterly report as "more eventful than expected", pointing to the Mailchimp divestiture at a loss and macroeconomic and AI-related pressures on Credit Karma.

The firm said Intuit would need to improve execution to regain investor confidence, although it sees an attractive risk-reward profile at current share prices.

UBS reduced its price target to $315 from $360 and maintained a Neutral rating.

The firm highlighted the Credit Karma slowdown, weaker second-quarter revenue guidance, AI disruption concerns, and moderating new-customer growth in Global Business Solutions.

Bank of America also cut its target to $310 from $360, reiterating its Neutral rating.

The brokerage pointed to a combination of cyclical and structural pressures affecting the company.

Wells Fargo similarly noted that resilient growth in Global Business Solutions and continued momentum in the mid-market segment were overshadowed by weaker-than-expected Credit Karma performance.

data.title: UK and EU strike post-Brexit reset deal, but tuition fee row remains unresolved
data.description:
The United Kingdom and the European Union have concluded negotiations on a series of agreements covering food and drink standards, emissions trading and youth mobility, marking a significant step towards resetting relations more than a decade after Brexit.

Downing Street confirmed on Friday that both sides had agreed on implementation timelines for a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement, a link between their emissions trading systems and a youth mobility scheme.

However, negotiations over tuition fees for European students attending British universities remain unresolved.

“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 spokesperson said, adding that the two sides would now work towards implementing the agreements.

“Now, both sides will work towards implementation of the youth mobility scheme, the SPS deal and the emissions trading scheme. Both sides have agreed when these will come into force. And those dates are set out in the joint statement, which will be published in due course."

“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place. And talks will continue on some areas – these will be set out in the joint statement later.”

The announcement came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham attended his first formal summit with the European Union in Brussels, where he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

Burnham said the broader package could add 0.5% to Britain's economy, while improving trading conditions for businesses and potentially easing pressure on consumers.

During the summit, he described the agreements as “a landmark agreement” that “will benefit every single person in the United Kingdom, but I would say in the European Union too,” according to the Press Association.

“For people struggling with the cost of living, this agreement holds out the real prospect that the cost of the weekly shop will begin to come down and Britain’s big supermarkets are saying that,” he said.

“For businesses struggling with the cost of doing business, this agreement will begin to reduce red tape and make it easier to do business and to export and that is good news for them.”

Food standards agreement expected to reduce trade barriers

A central component of the reset is an agreement to reduce regulatory checks and paperwork on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and the EU.

Under the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, Britain will align with EU agrifood standards, allowing agricultural and food products to move across borders with fewer checks and administrative requirements.

The arrangement is expected to take effect in 2028, according to multiple draft statements, and is estimated to deliver £5.1 billion ($6.7 billion) in economic benefits to the UK.

The agreement could provide relief to British food producers, exporters and retailers that have faced additional costs and administrative hurdles since the country left the EU's single market.

UK and EU agree to link emissions trading systems

The two sides have also reached an agreement to link their respective emissions trading systems, another important element of the post-Brexit reset.

The arrangement is intended to improve coordination between the UK and EU carbon markets and reduce additional costs for businesses operating across both jurisdictions.

However, the agreement will not immediately exempt British companies from the EU's carbon border taxes.

Overnight briefings indicated that the exemption would only take effect in 2028.

The development is particularly relevant for industries with significant carbon emissions and exposure to European trade, including steel, cement and other energy-intensive manufacturing sectors.

Linking the systems could help reduce regulatory differences and provide businesses with greater certainty as they navigate increasingly stringent climate-related trade requirements.

Youth mobility scheme to allow 100,000 people into UK annually

Another significant outcome of the negotiations is an agreement on a youth experience scheme (YES), which will allow young people to live and work in the UK and EU for a fixed period through lower-cost visas.

The proposed arrangement will allow up to 100,000 people annually to enter the UK, provided they are under the age of 32.

The scheme represents a limited relaxation of restrictions on movement introduced after Brexit, although it does not restore the freedom of movement that existed when Britain was part of the EU.

It is expected to create opportunities for young people seeking international work experience, education and cultural exchanges.

Burnham also highlighted cooperation on illegal immigration, pointing to Britain's participation in the Channel action plan.

“For people worried about illegal immigration, and there are many people who have very legitimate concerns about that, they will be pleased, I’m sure, to hear about Britain’s participation in the Channel action plan and that is a very significant step forward, sharing more data between us on that very important issue,” he said.

Tuition fees remain the biggest sticking point

Despite progress on the broader package, negotiations over tuition fees for European students studying in Britain remain unresolved.

The European Union has been pushing for students studying abroad to receive “equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees”, effectively requiring universities to charge EU students the same rates as domestic students.

Britain, however, has proposed an intermediate arrangement that would reduce fees without extending full home-fee status to European students.

According to two EU diplomats granted anonymity to discuss the negotiations, London has so far offered tuition fees of around £12,000, Politico reported.

That would represent a substantial reduction from the average £22,000 currently paid by EU students in Britain, although some courses charge considerably more.

It would also remain above the £9,790 paid by British students, the publication said.

The EU has raised concerns about the proposed arrangement because the fee reduction would be reciprocal.

One diplomat said it could require all 27 member states to introduce a separate tuition fee category for British students, Politico said.

Such a change could prove complicated, potentially requiring legislative amendments and adjustments to university funding systems in individual countries.

The disagreement has therefore emerged as one of the more difficult issues in an otherwise largely successful round of negotiations.

Nevertheless, both sides remain keen to present the agreements as a positive step in rebuilding relations and have expressed confidence that a compromise on tuition fees can eventually be reached.

For Britain, the agreements represent an attempt to secure some of the economic and administrative benefits of closer European integration without reversing its decision to leave the bloc.

The coming years will determine whether the reset translates into lower trade costs, stronger investment and a more predictable relationship between the two sides.

data.title: Oil price today: Brent pares losses after sliding to $90.06 amid Hormuz tensions
data.description:
Oil prices recovered from their session lows on Friday as traders weighed renewed security threats in the Strait of Hormuz against rising crude inventories and expectations of a global supply surplus.

January Brent futures were down 0.61% at $91.42 a barrel at 11:55 GMT, after briefly falling to $90.06 earlier in London trading. The contract settled at $91.98 on Thursday.

Actively traded January West Texas Intermediate futures slipped 0.25% to $82.23.

The partial recovery left Brent heading for a third consecutive weekly decline, highlighting the market's increasingly muted response to geopolitical threats.

What happened to oil prices today?

Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy claimed on Thursday that two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels of crude had struck mines and caught fire while navigating the Strait of Hormuz.

The vessels were not identified, and the alleged mine strikes remain independently unverified.

The Joint Maritime Information Center said in its latest advisory that no official or national authorities had confirmed Iran's claims.

However, the organisation documented four separate attacks in the strait over the preceding four days.

Among them was Wednesday's incident involving a tanker struck by an unidentified projectile near Khasab, Oman. The crew was reported safe.

Regional tensions intensified further on Friday when the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted five drones and a ballistic missile targeting the kingdom.

Despite those developments, Brent surrendered its initial gains, suggesting traders were reluctant to price in substantial additional supply losses without evidence of a sustained disruption.

Why did oil prices fall, then recover?

Oil's decline came alongside broader weakness in commodities.

The US dollar index traded around 103.89, close to its recent 19-month high, while gold and silver also recorded sharp losses.

Dollar strength makes crude more expensive for buyers using other currencies, potentially weakening demand.

Meanwhile, official US data showed commercial crude inventories increased by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million in the week ended 13 November.

Goldman Sachs oil researcher Daan Struyven has argued that exporters have become increasingly effective at managing the disruption through alternative pipelines, escorted shipping and ship-to-ship transfers.

Additional production outside the Persian Gulf and weaker Chinese demand have also helped soften the impact.

Goldman estimates the oil market moved into surplus in October and expects the excess to reach approximately 2 million barrels a day next year.

That supply outlook has made it harder for geopolitical developments alone to sustain a rally.

Can Brent hold above $90 before the OPEC+ meeting?

Goldman expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 before declining towards $78 late that year.

Its forecast assumes no major escalation causing lasting damage to Middle Eastern energy infrastructure.

The next important policy event comes on 29 November, when OPEC+ ministers meet to consider production arrangements for 2027.

Friday also marks the expiry of December WTI futures, making January the more actively traded contract.

Investors will additionally monitor the University of Michigan's final November consumer sentiment survey for clues about US economic demand and inflation expectations.

For those comparing the best commodity trading platforms, Friday's volatility illustrates why longer-term supply forecasts and immediate geopolitical risks need to be considered separately.

data.title: Anthropic IPO closes at $93.5B after full greenshoe, $119.5B with placement
data.description:
The Anthropic IPO has formally closed at $93.5 billion after underwriters bought every extra share they were allowed to, Anthropic said on 20 November 2026.

With a $26 billion private placement to seven chip and cloud groups alongside it, the total raised comes to about $119.5 billion.

The closing statement confirms 1,127,000,000 Class A shares sold at $83 each. That includes the full exercise of the underwriters' option to buy 147,000,000 additional shares from the company, the so-called greenshoe.

Anthropic IPO raise rises to $93.5 billion

When the deal priced on 18 November, the headline raise was about $81.3 billion from roughly 980 million shares. The greenshoe adds about $12.2 billion at the $83 offer price, an Invezz calculation, lifting gross proceeds to roughly $93.5 billion.

Of the 1.127 billion shares, 1,103,351,354 were sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 by existing stockholders. Anthropic received about $91.6 billion before underwriting discounts and expenses. The selling stockholders' portion, worth just under $2 billion at $83, does not go to the company.

That extends the Anthropic IPO's lead as the largest listing on record, ahead of SpaceX's debut in June. It also gives a newly public company one of the deepest cash cushions in the market as it scales up spending on computing power.

The $26bn private placement

Alongside the public offering, Anthropic closed the sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 price, for about $26.0 billion. The buyers were AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC Partners.

Those shares were sold in a private placement and were not registered under the Securities Act. They do not form part of the Class A stock that trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Including the selling stockholders, the IPO and the placement together raised about $119.5 billion before fees. Most of the companies that bought in are also Anthropic's suppliers of chips, memory, cloud capacity or manufacturing.

Who led the deal

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were the lead book-running managers. JPMorgan, Citigroup, Barclays, Wells Fargo Securities, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, RBC Capital Markets and UBS Investment Bank were also bookrunners.

A further seven banks acted as additional bookrunners and five as co-managers. The registration statement was declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission on 18 November, and the shares began trading the following day.

What the close means for ANT investors

A fully exercised greenshoe is usually a sign of strong demand. Underwriters normally sell extra shares at the outset and use the option to cover that position, which they tend to do in full when the stock trades above the offer price.

ANT did that on day one. The stock opened at $111.50 on 19 November and closed at $97.17, about 17% above the $83 offer price. At that close, the 1.127 billion IPO shares were worth roughly $109.5 billion, an Invezz calculation, a paper gain of about $16bn for buyers in the deal.

For the strategic investors, the 313 million Class N shares were worth about $4.4 billion more at Thursday's close than they paid, on the same basis. That cushion has been tested on Friday, as ANT fell about 10% in early trading amid a wider AI selloff, covered in our Anthropic stock price report for day two.

Morningstar, which holds a $92 fair value estimate on the stock, said the capital raised, together with $132 billion of cash on the balance sheet, should allow Anthropic to meet its compute commitments even if revenue growth stalls. Those commitments are one of the biggest questions hanging over the shares.

Lock-up and what to watch next

Insiders cannot sell freely straight away. The lock-up runs until after results for the third quarter of next year, Bloomberg News reported, which limits the supply of new stock that could reach the market in the near term.

The next catalysts are Anthropic's first quarterly report as a public company and the start of research coverage from the banks that ran the deal, which are restricted from publishing for a period after the IPO. Independent firms have already set targets, as tracked in our Anthropic stock forecast and ANT price target roundup.

For the full timeline, valuation and share structure, see our Anthropic IPO hub. If you are looking to trade the shares now that they are listed, our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock explains the options.

data.title: Nvidia stock falls for seventh day as Damodaran flags risks and $140 entry
data.description:
Nvidia stock NVDA fell 3% on Friday, extending its losing streak to seven consecutive sessions as the chipmaker faced renewed scrutiny over its China business and leadership transition.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday.

His office is examining whether the company or former chief executive Jensen Huang allowed advanced chips to reach China and misled investors.

The investigation adds to concerns surrounding the company following Huang's departure and allegations involving China.

Meanwhile, valuation expert and New York University professor Aswath Damodaran has identified $140 per share as a potential buying level, while warning that the leadership crisis and related developments could affect Nvidia's intrinsic value.

Damodaran identifies $140 as potential buying level

In a blog post, Damodaran, who is known as the 'Dean of Valuation', described Huang as a great CEO and said he would consider buying Nvidia shares if they fell below $140.

He estimated Nvidia's value at approximately $4.8 trillion and said he would seek a price around 30% below that valuation.

This would translate into a breakeven value of roughly $140 per share.

Damodaran said he had placed a limit buy order at that level and would add Nvidia back to his portfolio if the stock reached it.

However, he cautioned that the recent decline did not necessarily mean the shares had become cheap.

Nvidia's intrinsic value may have fallen because of the loss of its leader and the fallout from the controversy, he said.

Nvidia's market capitalisation has declined by more than $2 trillion to approximately $3.52 trillion since Huang first acknowledged an affair at the start of last week.

The company announced his resignation last Thursday and appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief.

China allegations remain a key risk

Damodaran identified the China-related allegations as a major uncertainty for Nvidia's valuation.

He said that if claims involving official Chinese government connections and chip sales through Asian business fronts proved true, the resulting legal and regulatory consequences could persist regardless of who leads the company.

The potential financial impact would depend on how the situation develops.

If the disruption from Huang's departure remains limited to short-term issues, including transition delays, margin pressure, and legal friction, Damodaran estimated that the impact on Nvidia's equity value could be contained to a 5% to 10% decline in most scenarios.

However, he warned that a broader strategic shift could have more significant consequences.

If Nvidia reduces its customer financing and ecosystem marketing efforts, its long-term revenue growth and margins could face greater pressure.

CEO succession adds to investor uncertainty

Nvidia's search for a permanent chief executive is another issue facing investors.

Damodaran considers Kress and other company insiders potential candidates.

However, he does not view Apple CEO Tim Cook as a suitable long-term choice for Nvidia, although he said Cook could potentially manage the company temporarily during a crisis.

He also highlighted the importance of corporate governance, arguing that even highly successful executives need appropriate oversight.

Meanwhile, Daiwa Securities reiterated its Outperform rating on Nvidia but lowered its price target to $185 from $245.

The brokerage said Nvidia's operating performance remained strong but identified two major concerns weighing on the shares: whether the scale of AI capital expenditure meant revenue and earnings growth were approaching a peak, and whether a new CEO could match Huang's leadership.

Daiwa said it did not believe Nvidia was nearing peak revenue or earnings as long as customers continued to generate returns from AI solutions.

However, the leadership question remains a significant uncertainty for investors as the company navigates its transition.

data.title: Anthropic stock forecast: ANT price targets point to 28% upside on average
data.description:
The first Anthropic stock forecast numbers from Wall Street point higher. Seven firms have published price targets on ANT, ranging from $100 to $155, and their average sits about 28% above Thursday's $97.17 close, on an Invezz calculation as of 20 November 2026.

Not everyone is convinced. Morningstar's fair value estimate is below the closing price, and Seaport Research has started coverage at Neutral without a target. The banks that underwrote the IPO have not yet published research.

Anthropic stock forecast: the price targets so far

The highest target comes from Melius Research. Analyst Ben Reitzes started ANT at Buy with a two-year target of $155, about 6 times his projected 2029 revenue of roughly $430bn. That implies about 60% upside from the first-day close.

Needham's Scott Berg rates the stock Buy with a $150 target, about 54% above the close. The target equals 18 times Needham's fiscal 2027 revenue estimate, and Berg sees a $5.6tn market if businesses redirect 10% of labour spending to generative AI.

Wolfe Research started at Outperform with a $135 target, about 39% upside. Analyst Alex Zukin called Anthropic "not only America's Next Top Model, but rather its next BEST business".

Citizens rates ANT Market Outperform with a $125 target, about 29% above the close. Analyst Patrick Walravens forecasts revenue of $52.5bn in 2026 and $137bn in 2027.

ANT price target list versus the $97.17 close

Upside figures below are Invezz calculations against the 19 November close of $97.17:

The simple average of the seven price targets is about $124.56, an Invezz calculation. Morningstar's $92 is a fair value estimate rather than a price target, so it is not included in that average.

The three lowest targets were set before the IPO priced, when the expected range was $70 to $78. Unless New Street, Freedom Broker and KGI revise them, they now sit only slightly above the closing price.

William Blair's $130 to $150 range

William Blair has started Anthropic at Outperform without a formal price target. Analysts led by Arjun Bhatia said a multiple of 17 to 20 times revenue "would not be unreasonable", implying a price of $130 to $150.

That range is about 34% to 54% above the close, an Invezz calculation. William Blair said the stock trades at 9 times its 2027 revenue estimate and 6 times 2028, and called Anthropic "a generational company driving a generational technology shift".

The fundamentals behind the targets

The bull cases rest on growth. Anthropic's run-rate revenue reached $81bn as of 31 October, according to its filings, about three years after its first commercial product.

Profitability is less settled. Anthropic reported an operating loss of $567m for the third quarter, which is why most targets are framed on revenue multiples rather than earnings.

The cautious calls

Morningstar has kept its $92 fair value estimate, about 5% below the close. It has a bull case of $188 and a bear case of $25, which shows how wide the range of outcomes still is for a company with more than $900bn of compute commitments.

Seaport Research's Jay Goldberg started at Neutral with no target. "Anthropic is an incredible company, but it is also asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors," he wrote, pointing to revenue growth that slowed sharply in the third quarter.

What the Anthropic stock forecast leaves out

Most of Wall Street has yet to weigh in. Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and the rest of the underwriting syndicate are restricted from publishing research for a period after the IPO. Their initiations, likely to arrive in the coming weeks, could reset the consensus. Index demand is another possible catalyst: ANT could be added to the Russell 1000 and Nasdaq-100 as soon as December if it qualifies, Bloomberg reported.

Targets also move with the market. ANT fell about 10% in early trading on Friday as an AI selloff hit Nvidia and AMD, which is covered in our Anthropic stock price report for day two. A weaker share price makes the existing targets look more generous, but it can also prompt analysts to revisit them.

The raise behind the stock is now final at $93.5bn, as set out in our report on the Anthropic IPO close. For the valuation history and timeline, see our Anthropic IPO hub, and for access to the shares, our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock.

Price targets are opinions, not guarantees. Anthropic's first quarterly report as a public company will be the first real test of these forecasts.

data.title: Anthropic stock price falls nearly 10% on day two as AI selloff hits ANT
data.description:
The Anthropic stock price fell about 10% in early trade on Friday 20 November 2026, its second day of trading, as a broad AI selloff dragged chip stocks lower.

ANT was at $87.90 at 14:34 GMT, down 9.5% from Thursday's $97.17 close but still above the $83 IPO price.

Anthropic stock price slides on day two

The stock opened at about $89.86 when US trading began at 14:30 GMT, roughly 7.5% below the first-day close. It then slipped to a low of $87.53 in the first few minutes.

About 73 million shares had traded by 14:34 GMT. These are early prints and will change through the session.

The shares had already been under pressure before the bell. ANT slipped about 5% in post-market trading on Thursday, Bloomberg reported, having traded as much as 39% above the IPO price earlier in the session.

It was down about 5.6% at 09:23 GMT in thin pre-market trade, and the losses deepened through the morning. By 14:07 GMT it was indicated at $88.31, about 9% below Thursday's close.

That reverses a large part of the debut gain. On Thursday, ANT opened at $111.50, traded between $92.72 and $115.10, and closed at $97.17, about 17% above the $83 IPO price. More than 846 million shares changed hands.

Why ANT is falling with Nvidia and AMD

The move is less about Anthropic itself than about the trade around it. Investors had hoped the record listing would revive AI stocks, which have been hit in recent months by concerns over how much companies are spending on data centres and chips.

Thursday's debut did not help: the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.2% on the day. Several other things have made the mood worse this week. Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, and Washington is moving to close an export-control loophole that could hit AI chip sales to Asia.

On Thursday, short seller Hunterbrook Media alleged that firmware sold by AMD had turned up at US-blacklisted companies, and AMD closed down more than 7%. AMD told CNBC it complies with US law.

There is a competitive worry too. Apple has said it is developing its own autonomous AI agent, a potential competitive threat to Anthropic's Claude.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee also released documents showing that a Commerce Department subagency approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, raising the prospect of a sales slowdown under tighter controls.

Chip stocks fell with it. At 14:34 GMT, Nvidia was down about 3.4% at around $141.07 and AMD was down about 6% at around $459.92, extending Thursday's losses.

The $83 IPO price is the level to watch

For buyers who got stock at $83 in the offering, the shares remain in profit. At $87.90, ANT was about 5.9% above the offer price, an Invezz calculation, but that cushion is much thinner than the 17% at Thursday's close or the 34% at the open.

There is also less of a safety net than in many listings. Anthropic has confirmed that underwriters exercised their option to buy all 147 million extra shares, taking the deal to $93.5bn. With the option used in full, banks no longer hold the short position that they can cover by buying stock in the market, a common source of support in an IPO's early days.

That said, insiders are still bound by a lock-up, which limits new supply for now. The details of the final raise and the $26bn placement to Nvidia, AMD and five others are in our report on the Anthropic IPO close.

What analysts expect

Friday's drop takes ANT further below most published targets. Melius Research has a $155 target and Needham $150, while Morningstar's $92 fair value estimate is close to where the stock is now trading. The full list is in our Anthropic stock forecast and ANT price target roundup.

A new listing of this size is likely to stay volatile while price discovery continues and the wider AI trade remains fragile. The next tests are how ANT closes its first week and when the underwriting banks begin publishing research.

For the valuation, share structure and timeline, see our Anthropic IPO hub. If you are weighing a trade after the pullback, our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock sets out how to get access.

data.title: Nasdaq falls as Anthropic slides, dragging AI stocks into weekly selloff
data.description:
US markets opened lower on Friday as Anthropic shares fell after its blockbuster debut, dashing investor hopes of it reviving the AI trade.

The AI lab's initial public offering and Nvidia's latest earnings were seen as key tests of whether battered investor confidence in artificial intelligence stocks could recover.

However, neither event was enough to restore enthusiasm after weeks of concerns about the profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs and regulatory risks.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened 100 points higher while the S&P 500 fell 0.46%. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.33%.

Anthropic shares fell 9.3% in trading after surging in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday.

The decline weighed on other AI-linked stocks, with Nvidia falling 3.66% and Advanced Micro Devices dropping 6.3%.

AI stocks extend weekly losses

The weakness in Anthropic shares added to a broader selloff in technology and semiconductor stocks.

Among major technology companies,

Amazon and Microsoft declined, while Meta fell 2.5% and Alphabet gained 1.45%.

Amazon and Alphabet are among Anthropic's biggest investors.

Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Marvell Technology and Micron fell between 2.6% and 7%.

Neocloud companies CoreWeave and Nebius also dropped 6% and 7%, respectively.

Data centre stocks were under pressure, with IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific falling approximately 7%.

Nvidia shares were down 3.6%, putting the chipmaker on track for its longest weekly losing streak since 2008.

The declines followed Thursday's broad market selloff, when all three major US indexes lost more than 2%.

The Dow closed below 50,000 for the first time since June, while the S&P 500 recorded its sixth consecutive daily loss, its longest losing streak since April 2024.

The Nasdaq was 13.6% below its October 6 record closing high as of Thursday's close.

For the week, the Dow had fallen 6.2%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were each down about 5%.

All three indexes were on track for their steepest weekly declines since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his Liberation Day tariffs.

The CBOE Volatility Index, commonly known as Wall Street's fear gauge, rose by three points to 30 on Friday, its highest level since March 30.

Inflation and Fed rate outlook in focus

Investors are also assessing the outlook for US interest rates after renewed concerns about persistent inflation.

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the central bank would need to raise interest rates again because inflation remained too high.

Markets are pricing in a 99.2% probability of an interest rate hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Attention will also be on a speech by Fed Governor Lisa Cook later on Friday.

Next week's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation figures could provide further clues about the central bank's monetary policy path, following a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Elsewhere, Intuit shares fell 5.1% after the company lowered its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion.

Intuit acquired the email marketing platform five years ago for nearly three times that amount.
